title: Proteomics and Mass Spectrometry Basics
markdown: ## What this covers This chapter introduces the fundamental concepts of mass spectrometry (MS) based proteomics. It outlines the core architecture of mass spectrometers—ion sources, mass analysers, and detectors—and details tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS) and collision-induced dissociation (CID) for peptide sequence analysis. The material assumes an elementary knowledge of biochemistry and basic physical principles of charged particles. ## Building Blocks: Amino Acids and Peptides Proteomics is the large-scale study of proteins: their structures, functions, modifications, and expression levels. Proteins are linear polymers assembled from 20 standard amino acids linked by covalent peptide bonds. An amino acid consists of a central alpha-carbon ($\text{C}_\alpha$) bonded to: - A basic amino group ($-\text{NH}_2$) - An acidic carboxyl group ($-\text{COOH}$) - A hydrogen atom ($-\text{H}$) - A distinctive side chain ($-\text{R}$) Peptide bond formation occurs via a condensation reaction between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of another, releasing a water molecule ($\text{H}_2\text{O}$, mass $\approx 18.01056\text{ Da}$). In bottom-up (shotgun) proteomics, intact proteins are digested enzymatically (typically using trypsin, which cleaves specifically C-terminal to lysine and arginine residues, unless followed by proline) into shorter peptides. These peptides are significantly more amenable to chromatographic separation, ionization, and gas-phase fragmentation than whole macromolecular proteins. ## Architecture of a Mass Spectrometer A mass spectrometer does not measure mass directly; it measures the mass-to-charge ratio ($m/z$) of gas-phase ions. Every mass spectrometer consists of three primary inline stages operating under high vacuum (to prevent collisions with background gas molecules): 1. **Ion Source**: Converts neutral analyte molecules in solution or solid state into gas-phase ions. 2. **Mass Analyser**: Separates or resolves ions according to their $m/z$ ratios using electromagnetic fields. 3. **Detector**: Measures the ion current produced by arriving or oscillating ions, converting ion abundance into an electronic signal. ### Ion Sources Biomolecules are non-volatile and thermally labile; classical heating causes degradation. Modern proteomics relies on soft ionization techniques: - **Electrospray Ionization (ESI)**: Operates at atmospheric pressure directly coupled to liquid chromatography (LC-MS). The peptide effluent passes through a capillary held at high electric potential ($2\text{--}5\text{ kV}$). As charged droplets evaporate, electrostatic repulsion (Coulomb fission) disperses the droplets down to gas-phase ions. ESI typically generates multiply charged ions ($[\text{M} + z\text{H}]^{z+}$, where $z \ge 2$), compressing the observed $m/z$ scale into the operating range of standard analysers. - **Matrix-Assisted Laser Desorption/Ionization (MALDI)**: The sample is co-crystallized with an organic matrix (such as $\alpha$-cyano-4-hydroxycinnamic acid). A pulsed laser irradiates the crystal, causing rapid ablation and energy transfer. The matrix transfers protons to the analyte, usually producing singly charged ions ($[\text{M} + \text{H}]^{+}$). ### Mass Analysers Different mass analysers use distinct physical phenomena to resolve ions by $m/z$: - **Quadrupole (Q)**: Employs four parallel cylindrical or hyperbolic rods with oscillating radiofrequency (RF) and direct current (DC) potentials. For a given set of voltages, only ions of a specific $m/z$ window have stable trajectories through the rods; other ions collide with the rods or exit the field. - **Time-of-Flight (TOF)**: Ions are accelerated by an electrostatic potential $V$ into a field-free drift tube of length $L$. The kinetic energy imparted is: $$E_k = z e V = \frac{1}{2} m v^2$$ The velocity is $v = \sqrt{\frac{2 z e V}{m}}$, yielding a drift time: $$t = \frac{L}{v} = L \sqrt{\frac{m}{2 z e V}}$$ Flight time $t$ scales with $\sqrt{m/z}$, allowing fast scanning across wide mass ranges. - **Orbitrap and Fourier Transform Ion Cyclotron Resonance (FT-ICR)**: High-resolution trapping instruments.
